Article.ArticleTitle: The Effect of Different L-carnitine Administration Routes on the Development of Atherosclerosis in ApoE Knockout Mice.

Abstract.AbstractText: L-carnitine (LC) is abundant in red meat and is widely added to health supplements and food. This study focused on the adverse effects of oral supplementation of 1.3% LC in ApoE-/- mice and whether the parenteral administration of LC (subcutaneously, sub) had any impact on the development of atherosclerosis.

Mice were randomly divided into 3 groups (n = 15). All mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD). The number of Ly6Chi monocytes; degree of atherosclerosis; plasma LC, γ-butyrobetaine (γBB) and trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) levels; and microbial community composition were analysed. Compared with the HFD and HFD+LC (sub) groups, the number of Ly6Chi monocytes, atherosclerotic plaque area and plasma γBB and TMAO levels were increased in the HFD+LC (oral) group (P<0.001). Plasma LC levels in the HFD+LC (sub) group were higher than those in other groups. The levels of γBB, TMAO and Ly6Chi monocytes were positively correlated with atherosclerotic plaque area (P<0.01), and TMAO was positively correlated with Bacteroidetes and negatively correlated with Firmicutes at the phylum level.

In contrast with oral LC administration, subcutaneous LC administration, which bypasses its conversion to TMAO in the liver, does not have a detrimental effect on the development of atherosclerosis in male ApoE-/- mice. Taking LC parenterally may be preferable among patients who require LC supplementation. This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
